title: Reading a pedigree: a bleeding disorder

stimulus.title: A family with a bleeding disorder
stimulus.text: The pedigree shows three generations of a family in which some members have a rare bleeding disorder caused by an allele of a single gene. Genetic testing later showed that the gene is on the X chromosome. II-4 married into the family and has no relatives with the disorder. Use XH for the allele for normal clotting and Xh for the allele that causes the disorder.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using evidence from the pedigree, explain why the disorder cannot be caused by a dominant allele.

rubric.point: Explains that affected individuals (II-2 or III-1) have two unaffected parents (I-1 and I-2, or II-3 and II-4); with a dominant allele, an affected person would have at least one affected parent.
accept: II-2 is affected but neither I-1 nor I-2 is, so the allele must be hidden in a parent
an affected child of two unaffected parents means the allele is recessive
III-1's parents are both unaffected; a dominant allele would show in the parent who passed it on

parts.sample: II-2 has the disorder, but neither of his parents (I-1 and I-2) does. If the allele were dominant, the parent who passed it to him would also have the disorder. So the allele must have been hidden in an unaffected parent, which means it is recessive.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the genotypes of I-2 and II-3, and describe the evidence in the pedigree for each.

rubric.point: Identifies both I-2 and II-3 as X<sup>H</sup>X<sup>h</sup> (carriers), because each is unaffected but has an affected son, and a son receives his only X from his mother (his father gives him a Y).
accept: both are heterozygous carriers, X^H X^h; their affected sons got X^h from them
I-2 passed X^h to II-2 and II-3 passed X^h to III-1, and both are unaffected, so heterozygous
carrier mothers: sons inherit the X from the mother

parts.sample: I-2 and II-3 are both X<sup>H</sup>X<sup>h</sup>. Each is unaffected, so each has at least one X<sup>H</sup>. Each also has an affected son (II-2 and III-1). A son gets his Y from his father and his only X from his mother, so each son's X<sup>h</sup> came from his mother. So both women are carriers.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the probability that III-2 is a carrier of the disorder.

rubric.point: Calculates 1/2 (0.5 or 50%): III-2 receives X<sup>H</sup> from her father (II-4, X<sup>H</sup>Y) and either X<sup>H</sup> or X<sup>h</sup> from her mother (II-3, X<sup>H</sup>X<sup>h</sup>), each with probability 1/2.
accept: 1/2, because her mother passes X^h half the time and her father always passes X^H
0.5 with a Punnett square of X^H X^h × X^H Y showing half the daughters are carriers

parts.sample: 1/2. Her father, II-4, is unaffected, so he is X<sup>H</sup>Y and gives every daughter X<sup>H</sup>. Her mother, II-3, is X<sup>H</sup>X<sup>h</sup> and gives X<sup>h</sup> with probability 1/2. So III-2 is X<sup>H</sup>X<sup>h</sup> (a carrier) with probability 1/2, and X<sup>H</sup>X<sup>H</sup> otherwise.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: III-2 plans to have children with a man who does not have the disorder. Predict the probability that their first son will have the disorder, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts 1/4 (25%) and justifies with the product rule: III-2 is a carrier with probability 1/2, and a carrier passes X<sup>h</sup> to a son with probability 1/2; the father gives a son only his Y, so he does not affect the son's risk.
accept: 1/4 = 1/2 (she is a carrier) × 1/2 (she passes X^h to the son)
25%, because the son's X comes from his mother, who is a carrier half the time and then passes X^h half the time
0.25; the father's X^H goes only to daughters

parts.sample: 1/4. A son gets his Y from his father, so his X, and his risk, depend only on III-2. She is a carrier with probability 1/2 (part c). If she is a carrier, she passes X<sup>h</sup> to a son with probability 1/2. Both must happen: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
